items.stem: In which stage of the program development life cycle are the requirements of the client identified?
items.answer: Analysis
items.markingKey: Analysis: investigate the problem, interview users, produce a requirements specification.

items.stem: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the waterfall model.
items.answer: Advantage: simple to manage with clear stages and documentation. Disadvantage: the client sees the product late, and changes to requirements are difficult/expensive.

items.stem: Explain why RAD may be suitable for a project where the requirements are not clear.
items.answer: Users see working prototypes early and give feedback, so requirements can be discovered and changed throughout development.

items.stem: A bank needs safety-critical software with fixed, well-understood requirements. Describe two activities in the analysis stage.
items.answer: Interviews, questionnaires, observation, document review; producing the requirements specification.

items.stem: City Central Library in Istanbul needs a booking app quickly but is not sure what features it wants. (a) Describe what happens in the maintenance stage. (b) Explain one drawback of RAD for this project.
items.answer: (a) Program is corrected, adapted or improved after release. (b) Less documentation; needs committed users; may not suit large or safety-critical systems.

items.stem: Noah is the project manager at Summit Engineering. Evaluate the choice of the waterfall model rather than rapid application development for the project at Summit Engineering.
items.answer: Points in favour: clear stages and documentation; easy to manage and budget; suits fixed, well-understood requirements and safety-critical systems. Points against / limitations: client sees product late; changes are costly; problems found late in testing; RAD gives early prototypes and feedback. Conclusion: waterfall suits stable requirements; RAD suits changing requirements and tight deadlines.

items.stem: What does a structure chart show?
options: The modules of a program, how they are related and the parameters passed between them
The truth table of a circuit
The order in which every instruction runs
The states of a system and transitions
items.answer: The modules of a program, how they are related and the parameters passed between them
items.markingKey: Structure charts show hierarchy and data flow between modules.

items.stem: Explain how a structure chart helps a programmer design a program.
items.answer: It shows how the problem is decomposed into modules, the hierarchy of calls and the parameters passed, so modules can be designed, coded and tested separately.

items.stem: Explain how a state-transition diagram can be used to design a vending machine program.
items.answer: It identifies every state (waiting, coins inserted, dispensing), the inputs/events that change state and the outputs, so the program logic covers every case.

items.stem: A state-transition table has the transitions S1 --a--> S2; S1 --b--> S3; S2 --a--> S3; S2 --b--> S3; S3 --a--> S1; S3 --b--> S2. The start state is S1. State the final state after the input sequence abbba.
items.answer: S1

items.stem: A state-transition table has the transitions S1 --a--> S3; S1 --b--> S2; S2 --a--> S2; S2 --b--> S1; S3 --a--> S2; S3 --b--> S3. The start state is S1. State the final state after the input sequence aabab, and the sequence of states visited.

A door entry system is modelled by the transitions S1 --a--> S3; S1 --b--> S3; S2 --a--> S1; S2 --b--> S1; S3 --a--> S1; S3 --b--> S3; S1 is the start state and S2 is the accepting state (door opens). (a) Give the states visited for the input abbba. (b) State whether the door opens. (c) Describe how this would be drawn as a state-transition diagram. (d) Explain one benefit of designing the system this way.
items.answer: (a) S1 → S3 → S3 → S3 → S3 → S1 (b) No (c) circles for states, labelled arrows for each transition, arrow into S1, double circle for S2 (d) every state/input combination is considered so the logic is complete

items.stem: On a structure chart, what does a curved arrow around the lines to sub-modules show?
items.answer: Iteration (the modules are repeated)
items.markingKey: A diamond shows selection; a curved arrow shows repetition.

items.stem: A team at Nova Telecom is planning a ticket machine. Explain why a state-transition diagram suits a ticket machine.
items.answer: The machine moves between a fixed set of states (waiting, paid, printing) in response to events, which the diagram shows.

items.stem: Daniel is designing a program for Atlas Museum using diagrams. Explain why parameters are shown on a structure chart.
items.answer: They show what data each module needs and returns, helping define module interfaces.

items.stem: Mohammed is designing a program for Nova Telecom using diagrams. (a) Explain why a state-transition diagram suits a ticket machine. (b) Explain what an arrow labelled "coin inserted" between two states means.
items.answer: (a) The machine moves between a fixed set of states (waiting, paid, printing) in response to events, which the diagram shows. (b) When the event "coin inserted" happens in the first state, the system moves to the second state.

items.stem: A team at Summit Engineering in Riyadh is designing a program using a structure chart. (a) Explain how iteration would be shown on the structure chart. (b) Explain how selection would be shown on the structure chart.
items.answer: (a) A curved arrow over the lines to the modules that are repeated. (b) A diamond on the line to the module that is only called if a condition is true.

items.stem: A door entry system is modelled by the transitions S1 --a--> S2; S1 --b--> S2; S2 --a--> S2; S2 --b--> S3; S3 --a--> S2; S3 --b--> S1; S1 is the start state and S3 is the accepting state (door opens). (a) Give the states visited for the input bbaab. (b) State whether the door opens. (c) Describe how this would be drawn as a state-transition diagram. (d) Explain one benefit of designing the system this way.
items.answer: (a) S1 → S2 → S3 → S2 → S2 → S3 (b) Yes (c) circles for states, labelled arrows for each transition, arrow into S1, double circle for S3 (d) every state/input combination is considered so the logic is complete

items.stem: What is a syntax error?
options: A statement that breaks the grammar rules of the programming language
An error that only occurs when the program runs
A spelling mistake in a comment
An error in the logic of the program
items.answer: A statement that breaks the grammar rules of the programming language
items.markingKey: Syntax errors are found by the translator; the program will not run.

items.stem: Explain the difference between white-box and black-box testing.
items.answer: White-box testing uses knowledge of the code to test every path/branch; black-box testing checks outputs for given inputs against the specification without looking at the code.

items.stem: Explain why acceptance testing is carried out.
items.answer: The client checks that the finished system meets the agreed requirements before formally accepting (and paying for) it.

items.stem: A program accepts a test mark between 24 and 78 inclusive. Which type of test data is the value 78?
items.answer: extreme
items.markingKey: Normal: within range; extreme: 24 or 78; boundary: 23/24 and 78/79; abnormal: outside range or wrong type.

items.stem: Grace is testing a program for TransGlobal Logistics that accepts a age between 13 and 28 inclusive. Give one example each of normal, extreme, abnormal and boundary test data, with the expected outcome.
items.answer: Normal: 22 (accepted); extreme: 13 or 28 (accepted); abnormal: e.g. 43 or "abc" (rejected); boundary: 12 rejected / 13 accepted (or 28 accepted / 29 rejected)
items.markingKey: 1 mark per correct type with expected outcome [4]

items.stem: Sofia is testing a program for Eagles Sports Club that accepts a room temperature between 41 and 52 inclusive. Give one example each of normal, extreme, abnormal and boundary test data, with the expected outcome.
items.answer: Normal: 46 (accepted); extreme: 41 or 52 (accepted); abnormal: e.g. 67 or "abc" (rejected); boundary: 40 rejected / 41 accepted (or 52 accepted / 53 rejected)
items.markingKey: 1 mark per correct type with expected outcome [4]

items.stem: Noah has finished coding a program that calculates staff overtime pay for Nova Telecom. (a) Describe the difference between alpha and beta testing for this system. (b) Explain why white-box testing is used by the developers.
items.answer: (a) Alpha: in-house by the developers/testers; beta: by selected real users in their own environment before release. (b) Every path/branch in the code is tested so hidden logic errors are found.

items.stem: Riverside Medical Centre in Istanbul has commissioned a new online booking system. (a) Describe the difference between alpha and beta testing for this system. (b) Explain how a dry run with a trace table could find a logic error.
items.answer: (a) Alpha: in-house by the developers/testers; beta: by selected real users in their own environment before release. (b) Work through the algorithm by hand recording each variable; compare with expected values; find the line where they differ.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark per point, max 3 [3]

items.stem: What is a logic error?
options: An error that stops the program from being translated
An error that causes the program to give incorrect results even though it runs
items.answer: An error that causes the program to give incorrect results even though it runs

items.stem: Explain why a program with no syntax errors may still contain errors.
items.answer: Logic errors (wrong results) and run-time errors (crashes) are not detected by the translator.

items.stem: A test team at FreshFarm Foods in Colombo is planning tests for a booking system. (a) Explain why extreme test data is used. (b) Explain why abnormal test data is used.
items.answer: (a) It checks that values at the limits of the valid range are accepted, where off-by-one errors are common. (b) It checks that invalid data is rejected rather than crashing the program or giving wrong results.

items.stem: A program accepts a number of tickets between 8 and 49 inclusive. Which type of test data is the value 50?
items.answer: boundary (just outside the range)
items.markingKey: Normal: within range; extreme: 8 or 49; boundary: 7/8 and 49/50; abnormal: outside range or wrong type.

items.stem: What type of error is shown by: Average ← Total / Count  (when no values have been entered)?
items.answer: run-time error
items.markingKey: division by zero when Count is 0.

items.stem: A program accepts a number of tickets between 44 and 119 inclusive. Which type of test data is the value 119?
items.answer: extreme
items.markingKey: Normal: within range; extreme: 44 or 119; boundary: 43/44 and 119/120; abnormal: outside range or wrong type.

items.stem: Identify the type of error in the statement DECLARE Name : STRNG and explain how it would be detected.
items.answer: Syntax error: misspelt keyword/data type.
items.markingKey: 1 mark type; 1 mark explanation; 1 mark detection method (translator for syntax; testing/dry run/trace for logic; crash during execution for run-time) [3]

items.stem: Elena has finished coding a program that calculates staff overtime pay for GreenLeaf Pharmacy. (a) Describe the difference between alpha and beta testing for this system. (b) Explain the purpose of acceptance testing.
items.answer: (a) Alpha: in-house by the developers/testers; beta: by selected real users in their own environment before release. (b) Client confirms the system meets the requirements specification.

items.stem: Amara has finished coding a program that calculates staff overtime pay for SwiftCar Rentals. (a) Describe a test plan for the system. (b) Explain the purpose of acceptance testing.
items.answer: (a) Lists each test, its purpose, test data (normal, extreme, abnormal), expected outcome, actual outcome. (b) Client confirms the system meets the requirements specification.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per feature, max 3 [3] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is corrective maintenance?
options: Fixing errors found after the program has been released
Changing the program for a new operating system
items.answer: Fixing errors found after the program has been released
items.markingKey: Corrective: bugs that were not found in testing.

items.stem: What is adaptive maintenance?
options: Changing a program to meet new requirements or a new environment
items.answer: Changing a program to meet new requirements or a new environment
items.markingKey: e.g. new law, new tax rate, new operating system or hardware.

items.stem: Explain why good documentation and meaningful identifiers make maintenance easier.
items.answer: Programmers who did not write the code can understand what each part does, so they can find and change the right code quickly with fewer new errors.

items.stem: Software used by City Central Library is changed. The report screen is redesigned so it loads twice as fast. Which type of maintenance is this?
items.answer: perfective

items.stem: The payroll program at Lakeside College in Seoul was released two years ago. Explain how the original programmer could have made maintenance easier.
items.answer: Comments, meaningful identifiers, modular design, documentation, consistent indentation.

items.stem: What is perfective maintenance?
options: Changing the program because of a new law
Improving the performance or usability of a program that already works
items.answer: Improving the performance or usability of a program that already works

items.stem: Identify the type of maintenance in each case, giving a reason: (1) A loop that occasionally never ends is corrected. (2) Users report the program crashes when a date in February is entered. (3) A search feature is made easier to use after user feedback.
items.answer: (1) corrective; (2) corrective; (3) perfective
items.markingKey: 1 mark per correct type with reason [3]

items.stem: Identify the type of maintenance in each case, giving a reason: (1) The report screen is redesigned so it loads twice as fast. (2) The code is optimised to use less memory. (3) A search feature is made easier to use after user feedback.
items.answer: (1) perfective; (2) perfective; (3) perfective
items.markingKey: 1 mark per correct type with reason [3]

items.stem: Mei has been asked to maintain a stock control program written by another programmer at TransGlobal Logistics. (a) Describe one example each of corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance for this program. (b) Explain why maintenance can cost more than the original development.
items.answer: (a) Corrective: fix a calculation bug; adaptive: new tax rules/OS; perfective: faster reports/better interface. (b) Programs are used for many years; changes needed repeatedly; programmers must first understand old code; new errors may be introduced.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) 1 mark per point, max 2 [2]

items.answer: Colleagues read the code and logic directly, so they can spot problems on paths that the test data does not exercise.

items.answer: A logic error gives wrong results but the program runs; a run-time error causes the program to stop/crash.

items.answer: (a) The environment or requirements change (new law, hardware, OS), so the program must be changed to keep working. (b) Changes may introduce new errors; regression testing checks that existing features still work.

items.stem: Software used by Palm Grove Hotel is changed. The app is updated to run on a new version of the operating system. Which type of maintenance is this?

items.stem: Tomás has finished coding a program that calculates staff overtime pay for Palm Grove Hotel. (a) Describe the difference between alpha and beta testing for this system. (b) Explain the purpose of acceptance testing. (c) Explain why white-box testing is used by the developers.
items.answer: (a) Alpha: in-house by the developers/testers; beta: by selected real users in their own environment before release. (b) Client confirms the system meets the requirements specification. (c) Every path/branch in the code is tested so hidden logic errors are found.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: The software used by GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Mumbai needs to be changed. Explain the difference between corrective and perfective maintenance.
items.answer: Corrective fixes errors; perfective improves a program that already works (speed, usability).

items.stem: Jonas maintains a program written several years ago for BlueWave Supermarkets. (a) Explain the difference between corrective and perfective maintenance. (b) Explain why adaptive maintenance may be needed even when the program has no errors.
items.answer: (a) Corrective fixes errors; perfective improves a program that already works (speed, usability). (b) The environment or requirements change (new law, hardware, OS), so the program must be changed to keep working.

items.stem: Software used by Coral Bay Aquarium is changed. A loop that occasionally never ends is corrected. Which type of maintenance is this?
items.answer: corrective
